lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
In metal furniture making, design and drawing are not optional luxuriesâthey are the foundation of every profitable job. Without a clear drawing, you waste metal, time, and money. In Africa, where steel and welding rods are costly, a simple sketch can save you thousands of shillings. Imagine a client in Nairobi ordering a set of six dining chairs. If you guess the dimensions, you might cut legs too short or too long, ending up with unstable chairs and an angry customer. But if you draw each part to scale, you calculate exactly how many metres of square tube you need, how many welding rods, and how many hours. That means you can quote a fair price and still make a profit.

Drawing also helps you communicate with your client. Many customers cannot read technical blueprints, but they understand a simple isometric sketch showing the front, side, and top views. You can mark dimensions in millimetres and point to where the seat will be, how high the backrest goes, and where the armrests attach. This avoids arguments later. In workshops from Accra to Johannesburg, the best welders always start with a pencil and paper. They draw the furniture piece at full size or to a scale like 1:10, using a ruler, set square, and compass. Even a rough drawing on cardboard is better than no drawing.

Finally, design thinking lets you add value. You can modify a standard design to use locally available materialsâlike using offcuts from a construction site or adapting to a clientâs small room. A good drawing also serves as a record. If a client wants a second identical chair six months later, you can pull out the drawing and repeat the job exactly. So treat design and drawing as your first tool, not an afterthought. It costs almost nothing but pays you back in saved materials, satisfied customers, and repeat business.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To draw metal furniture designs, you need a few basic tools. Most are cheap and available in any African town. Start with a drawing board or a flat piece of plywood at least 60 cm by 90 cm. You can make one yourself from a 12 mm plywood offcut. Cover it with a smooth sheet of paper taped down. For drawing, use a 2H pencil for fine lines and an HB pencil for darker lines. A pencil sharpener and eraser are essential. A 30 cm steel ruler with millimetre markings is your most important measuring tool. Also get a 60-degree set square and a 45-degree set square to draw perpendicular and angled lines. A compass for circles (like for round table tops) and a protractor for angles are useful.

For scale drawings, you need a scale ruler or simply use your steel ruler and divide by 10 for a 1:10 scale. For example, 1 metre becomes 10 cm on paper. Use A3 or A2 paper if you can get it; otherwise, tape two A4 sheets together. Graph paper is excellent because it already has a gridâeach square can represent 10 cm. For marking metal before cutting, you will need a scriber (a sharp steel point) or a permanent marker, a centre punch, and a hammer. A try square is used to check 90-degree angles on metal. A chalk line or soapstone is good for marking on dark metal.

Materials for drawing include pencils, erasers, masking tape, and paper. For the actual furniture, you will draw the metal sections: square tubes (e.g., 25 mm x 25 mm x 1.5 mm wall thickness), rectangular tubes (20 mm x 40 mm), round tubes (e.g., 25 mm diameter), and flat bars (e.g., 25 mm x 3 mm). You also need to know the standard lengths: usually 6 metres. When drawing, always note the material type, size, and length for each part. A simple materials list on the drawing helps you calculate cost. For example, a chair might need 3.2 m of 25x25 square tube, 1.5 m of 20x40 rectangular tube, and 0.5 m of flat bar. Keep your tools in a tin or pouch so they donât get lost. A clean, organised drawing kit makes your work faster and more accurate.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to draw a simple metal chair. First, decide the overall dimensions. A standard dining chair is 450 mm wide, 450 mm deep, and 900 mm high at the backrest. Seat height is 450 mm. Write these numbers down. Second, choose a scale. For a chair, 1:10 is goodâso 450 mm becomes 45 mm on paper. Use your ruler to mark a horizontal line for the floor. Third, draw the front view. Start with the two front legs: they are vertical lines 450 mm apart (45 mm on paper). The seat is a horizontal line at 450 mm height. The back legs go up to 900 mm. Add the backrest top rail. Use your set square to keep lines perpendicular. Fourth, draw the side view. Show the depth: front leg to back leg is 450 mm. The seat is at 450 mm. The backrest leans back slightly, maybe 100 mm offset at the top. Fifth, draw the top view (plan). This shows the seat frame: a rectangle 450 mm x 450 mm. Mark where the legs attach at the corners. Now add dimensions: use arrows and numbers. For example, write '450' between the front legs. Sixth, make a parts list. For each part, note the material, size, and length. For example: front legs (2 off) 25x25 square tube, 450 mm long. Back legs (2 off) 25x25 square tube, 900 mm long. Seat rails (4 off) 20x40 rectangular tube, 450 mm long. Seat slats (5 off) 25x3 flat bar, 450 mm long. Seventh, check your drawing. Does everything add up? Are the angles correct? Use a scale ruler to verify. Finally, transfer the drawing to a clean sheet or cardboard template. You can cut out cardboard pieces to test the fit before cutting metal. This step-by-step method works for tables, beds, and shelves tooâjust change the dimensions.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Even experienced welders make drawing mistakes. Here are the most common and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Not drawing to scale. If you sketch freehand, proportions will be wrong. Fix: Always use a ruler and a scale. For example, if you draw a chair 10 cm tall on paper but the seat is only 2 cm from the floor, the real chair will have a seat at 200 mmâtoo low. Fix by measuring twice. Mistake 2: Forgetting wall thickness. When you draw a 25 mm square tube, the inside is smaller. If you need a sliding fit, account for the 1.5 mm wall. Fix: Draw the outside dimensions and note the wall thickness in the parts list. Mistake 3: Ignoring weld gaps. Metal expands when heated. If you draw parts to butt together perfectly, after welding they may distort. Fix: Leave a 1-2 mm gap for weld penetration, or design with overlapping joints. Mistake 4: Not checking for square. A drawing might look right but if the diagonals of a rectangle are not equal, the frame will be twisted. Fix: Always draw and measure both diagonalsâthey must be equal. Mistake 5: Using the wrong pencil. A hard pencil (like 4H) makes faint lines that are hard to see; a soft pencil (like 2B) smudges. Fix: Use 2H for construction lines and HB for final lines. Mistake 6: Forgetting the clientâs space. You draw a table 1.2 m x 0.8 m, but the clientâs doorway is only 0.7 m wide. Fix: Always ask for room dimensions and door widths before drawing. Mistake 7: No allowance for feet or floor unevenness. Fix: Add adjustable feet or design legs with a 10 mm tolerance. Mistake 8: Losing the drawing. Fix: Keep a folder or take a photo with your phone. In Africa, many workshops now use WhatsApp to share drawings with clients for approval before cutting metal. That simple step prevents costly errors.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in design and drawing might seem oddâafter all, you are just sitting at a table. But poor drawings lead to dangerous furniture. A chair that collapses because you forgot to brace the legs can injure someone. So safety starts with the drawing. First, always design for stability. A table with a narrow base will tip over. Rule of thumb: the base should be at least 2/3 the height of the table. For a 750 mm high table, the base should be at least 500 mm wide. Second, avoid sharp edges in your design. Round off corners or specify a radius (e.g., 5 mm) on flat bar ends. Third, consider weight. A metal bed frame that is too heavy is hard to move and can fall on someone. Use thinner wall thickness where possible, like 1.2 mm instead of 2 mm, if strength allows. Fourth, think about fire safety. If you design a braai stand or stove, keep combustible materials away. Draw a heat shield.

Best practice includes clear, neat drawings. Use a title block with your name, date, scale, and clientâs name. Number each part and list them in a table. Use standard symbols: a circle with a cross for a hole, a zigzag line for a weld. Always draw the front, side, and top views. If the piece is complex, add an isometric view. Check your dimensions twice. Use a scale ruler, not a tape measure, for drawings. Keep your drawing board clean and dry. Store drawings flat, not rolled, to avoid creases. When marking metal, use a scriber and engineerâs blue (layout fluid) for accuracy. If you donât have engineerâs blue, use a permanent marker. Always wear safety glasses when cutting or grinding, but also when marking metalâtiny chips can fly. Finally, get a second pair of eyes. Ask a fellow welder to check your drawing for obvious mistakes. In many African workshops, apprentices learn by copying the masterâs drawings. That is good, but always verify with a ruler. A safe design is a profitable design because it prevents accidents, returns, and bad reviews.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now itâs your turn. In this exercise, you will draw a simple metal stool. A stool is a good beginner project because it has few parts but teaches all the basics. Follow these steps. Step 1: Gather your tools: A3 paper, pencil, ruler, set square, eraser, and a scale ruler (or your steel ruler). Step 2: Decide dimensions. A standard stool is 300 mm wide, 300 mm deep, and 450 mm high. Seat is 300 mm x 300 mm. Step 3: Choose scale 1:5. So 300 mm becomes 60 mm, and 450 mm becomes 90 mm. Step 4: Draw the front view. Draw a horizontal floor line. Draw two vertical lines 60 mm apart (these are the legs). They go up 90 mm. Draw a horizontal line at 90 mm for the seat. Add a stretcher (a horizontal bar) halfway up, at 45 mm. Step 5: Draw the side view. Same dimensions: 60 mm wide, 90 mm high. Show the seat depth. Step 6: Draw the top view. A square 60 mm x 60 mm. Mark the four corners where legs attach. Step 7: Add dimensions. Use arrows and numbers. Write '300' for width, '300' for depth, '450' for height. Step 8: Make a parts list. Use 25x25 square tube for legs (4 off, 450 mm long). Use 20x20 square tube for seat frame (4 off, 300 mm long). Use 25x3 flat bar for seat slats (3 off, 300 mm long). Use 20x20 square tube for stretchers (4 off, 300 mm long). Step 9: Check your drawing. Measure the diagonals of the top viewâthey must be equal (84.85 mm on paper). Step 10: Transfer to cardboard. Cut cardboard pieces to represent each tube and assemble a model. This will show you if the design works. If the stool looks unstable, widen the base to 350 mm. Step 11: Present your drawing to your instructor or a fellow learner for feedback. Ask: Is it clear? Are dimensions correct? Would you build from this? Step 12: If you have a client, show them the drawing and get approval before cutting metal. That is the professional way. Repeat this exercise with a small table (600 mm x 600 mm x 750 mm) to practice more.

quiz.q: Why is design and drawing important in metal furniture making?
options: A) It makes the work look professional
B) It saves materials and money
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: A clear drawing helps calculate exact material needs, reducing waste and cost.

quiz.q: What is a good scale for drawing a dining chair?
quiz.explanation: 1:10 is practical for furniture, making a 450 mm chair 45 mm on paper.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to draw circles in a design?
quiz.explanation: A compass is specifically designed for drawing circles and arcs.

quiz.q: What does a 2H pencil produce?
quiz.explanation: 2H is a hard pencil that gives fine, light lines for construction.

quiz.q: Which view shows the depth of a chair?
quiz.explanation: The side view shows the depth (front-to-back dimension).

quiz.q: What should you check to ensure a rectangular frame is square?
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals confirm the frame is square and not twisted.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when drawing metal furniture?
quiz.explanation: Wall thickness affects inside dimensions and fit; it must be noted.

quiz.q: What safety issue can arise from a poor drawing?
options: A) The furniture may be too heavy
C) The furniture may be too light
D) The furniture may be too expensive
quiz.explanation: Missing braces or wrong dimensions can lead to structural failure.

quiz.q: What is a good rule for table base width relative to height?
options: D) Base can be any width
quiz.explanation: A base at least 2/3 the height prevents tipping.

quiz.q: What scale is used in the practical exercise for a stool?
quiz.explanation: The exercise specifies 1:5 scale, so 300 mm becomes 60 mm.

quiz.q: What is the standard length of metal tubes in many African markets?
quiz.explanation: Steel tubes are commonly sold in 6-metre lengths.

quiz.q: Which pencil is recommended for final drawing lines?
quiz.explanation: HB gives a darker, clearer line for final drawings without smudging too much.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a centre punch?
options: B) To mark metal for drilling
quiz.explanation: A centre punch makes a small indentation to guide a drill bit.

quiz.q: Why should you leave a small gap between parts in a drawing?
options: A) To allow for weld penetration
C) To make it look neat
quiz.explanation: A 1-2 mm gap allows the weld to penetrate fully for a strong joint.

quiz.q: What is an isometric view?
options: A) A flat view from above
B) A 3D view showing three sides
quiz.explanation: Isometric shows the object in 3D, with three axes at 120 degrees.

quiz.q: What should a title block on a drawing include?
quiz.explanation: A title block identifies the drawing with key details like name, date, and scale.

quiz.q: What is a scriber used for?
quiz.explanation: A scriber is a sharp steel point for marking lines on metal.

quiz.q: What is the seat height of a standard dining chair?
quiz.explanation: Standard seat height is 450 mm for comfort.

quiz.q: Why is it important to ask for room dimensions before drawing?
options: B) To ensure the furniture fits
D) To select the metal type
quiz.explanation: Furniture must fit through doors and into the intended space.

quiz.q: What is a common fix for a drawing that is not to scale?
options: A) Redraw using a ruler and scale
quiz.explanation: Always use a ruler and a consistent scale to correct proportions.

quiz.q: What does a zigzag line on a drawing represent?
quiz.explanation: A zigzag line is a standard symbol for a weld.

quiz.q: Why should you keep drawings flat?
options: C) To make them look nice
quiz.explanation: Creases can distort measurements and make the drawing hard to read.

quiz.q: What is engineer's blue used for?
quiz.explanation: Engineer's blue is a layout fluid that makes scribed lines visible on metal.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: You must gather all drawing tools before starting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a parts list?
options: B) To list each part with material and size
quiz.explanation: A parts list helps calculate material requirements and cost.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when drawing a table?
options: A) Forgetting the client's doorway width
quiz.explanation: Furniture must fit through doors; always check access dimensions.

quiz.q: What is the recommended scale for a stool in the exercise?
quiz.explanation: 1:5 makes a 300 mm stool 60 mm on paper, easy to draw.

quiz.q: Why should you use a set square?
quiz.explanation: A set square ensures 90-degree angles are accurate.

quiz.q: What is a safe design practice for metal furniture?
quiz.explanation: Rounded corners reduce injury risk and look better.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of sharing a drawing via WhatsApp with a client?
options: B) It gets quick approval and prevents errors
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Digital sharing allows fast feedback and approval before cutting metal.
